summary: Describes Protocol Independent Multicast-Sparse Mode, a protocol for efficiently routing to multicast groups that may span wide-area and inter-domain networks. This experimental version was replaced by RFC 4601 and RFC 5059.

eli5.summary: A way to send one message to a big group, such as a live show, without sending a separate copy to everyone.

questions: how does sparse mode multicast work
how do routers join multicast groups
difference between shared and shortest-path trees
subtitle: A protocol for efficiently routing multicast traffic across wide-area networks using explicit group membership.

tldr.problem: Simple multicast protocols flood traffic to all routers in a network and let routers prune branches they do not need. This works in small, dense networks but wastes bandwidth and router resources in wide-area networks with sparse groups.
tldr.mechanism: PIM-SM (Sparse Mode) assumes multicast groups are sparse: receivers are scattered and not all routers need to carry traffic for every group. Routers explicitly join multicast trees using Join/Prune messages sent toward a Rendezvous Point or source. Traffic initially follows a shared tree rooted at the RP, and routers can switch to direct source-specific trees for high-bandwidth sources.
tldr.outcome: PIM-SM became the standard for interdomain multicast routing. This experimental version was succeeded by RFC 4601 and RFC 5059, which refined the protocol and addressed lessons from deployment.

today: RFC 2362 is Experimental. The protocol was further refined and standardized in RFC 4601 (PIM-SM v2) and RFC 5059 (PIM-SM extensions), which became the widely deployed multicast routing standard.

sections.title: Protocol Independent Multicast-Sparse Mode
sections.content:
RFC 2362 describes Protocol Independent Multicast-Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), a protocol for routing to multicast groups across wide-area and inter-domain networks. The term protocol independent means that PIM-SM does not depend on any particular unicast routing protocol; it works with any underlying IP routing.

The term sparse mode reflects the assumption that multicast groups have a small number of receivers scattered across the network, rather than being densely distributed everywhere. This design choice allows PIM-SM to scale to thousands of groups without flooding traffic everywhere. Unlike dense-mode protocols (such as DVMRP) that flood first and prune later, PIM-SM starts with no multicast forwarding and only builds distribution trees in response to explicit Join requests from receivers.
sections.eli5: PIM-SM is for big networks with groups that have receivers in distant places. Instead of sending everything everywhere, routers only forward to places that ask for it.

sections.title: Core Concepts and Terminology
sections.content:
A multicast group is identified by a group address (G), and a multicast source is identified by (S,G)—a combination of source address and group. Each group is assigned a Rendezvous Point (RP), a router that acts as a central meeting point.

The Designated Router (DR) on each subnet is the router responsible for discovering multicast receivers (via IGMP) and sending Join/Prune messages upstream. All routers maintain multicast route entries that specify the incoming interface and outgoing interfaces for forwarding packets.

PIM-SM uses two types of distribution trees: RP-rooted shared tree (denoted (*,G)) reaches all sources for a group through the RP, and source-specific shortest path tree (denoted (S,G)) forwards directly from the source to receivers via the shortest unicast path. The notation (*,G) means 'any source, group G'; (S,G) means 'source S, group G'.
sections.eli5: Groups have an RP (the central post office). Each subnet has a DR (the local representative). Trees are either shared (all sources through one point) or direct (from source to receiver).

sections.title: Distribution Trees and Message Flow
sections.content:
When a host joins a multicast group, the DR receives an IGMP membership indication and creates or updates a (*,G) route entry. The DR then sends a Join message toward the RP, creating the shared tree. Routers along the path toward the RP add the upstream interface (toward RP) and the incoming interface from the downstream DR to their route entries, building a tree rooted at the RP.

When a host sends to the group, its DR initially encapsulates the data packets in Register messages and unicasts them to the RP. The RP decapsulates and forwards the data down the shared tree to all receivers. If the data rate is high, the RP can send a Join message toward the source, causing the source's DR to send unencapsulated packets directly toward the RP. This allows routers between the source and RP to build (S,G) state and forward source-specific shortest-path traffic.

Routers with local receivers can switch from the shared tree to a source-specific shortest-path tree for high-bandwidth sources by creating (S,G) route entries and sending source-specific Join messages toward the source. Once the shortest-path tree is up, they send Prune messages toward the RP to stop receiving duplicates over the shared tree.
sections.eli5: When someone joins a group, their router asks the RP for the group's traffic. When someone sends, the RP gets it and forwards it. Later, receivers can ask to get the traffic directly from the sender instead of going through the RP.

sections.title: Protocol Messages and Mechanisms
sections.content:
Join/Prune messages are the workhorse of PIM-SM. A router sends a Join to add itself to a tree toward the RP or source, and a Prune to remove itself. These messages are sent periodically to maintain state and adapt to topology changes. Routers can merge multiple Join/Prune requests into a single message for efficiency.

Register messages carry the first data packets from a source to the RP, encapsulated so the RP knows which source is sending. The RP sends Register-Stop messages to stop Register traffic once it has joined the source's tree.

Bootstrap messages are used to discover Rendezvous Points. A router elected as the Bootstrap Router (BSR) periodically sends Bootstrap messages throughout the domain announcing a set of candidate RPs (C-RPs). Each router uses a hash function to map a group address to one of the announced RPs.

Hello messages allow neighboring routers to discover each other and elect a Designated Router on each subnet (the router with the highest IP address wins).
sections.eli5: Join says 'send me this traffic.' Prune says 'stop sending me this.' Register brings traffic to the RP. Bootstrap messages say 'here are the RPs.' Hellos let routers find each other.

sections.title: Tree Optimization and Multi-access Networks
sections.content:
A critical optimization in PIM-SM is the ability to switch from the shared RP-tree to a source-specific shortest-path tree. This is important because the RP may be far from receivers, causing unnecessary delay and bandwidth consumption. Once a router receives high-bandwidth source traffic over the shared tree, it can create a (S,G) route entry and join the source's tree directly. For low-bandwidth sources, the shared tree remains efficient.

On multi-access networks (like LANs with multiple routers), routers must coordinate to avoid duplicate forwarding. Assert messages allow routers to negotiate which one will forward data from a source. The router with the shortest distance to the source wins and becomes the forwarder. The others prune the interface.

When unicast routing changes (e.g., due to link failures), all route entries must have their incoming interface rechecked using Reverse Path Forwarding (RPF). If the new incoming interface appears in the outgoing interface list, it is removed to prevent loops.
sections.eli5: Routers optimize by switching to direct paths when traffic is heavy. When multiple routers are on the same network, they pick one to forward to avoid duplicates. When network paths change, routers update where they expect traffic from.

sections.title: Interoperability and Status
sections.content:
PIM-SM is designed to interoperate with dense-mode protocols like DVMRP across network boundaries. Special routers called Multicast Border Routers (PMBRs) bridge between PIM-SM domains and dense-mode domains. PMBRs maintain special (*,*,RP) state to pull all traffic originating within the PIM domain to the border and re-inject externally-originated traffic into the domain.

RFC 2362 specifies PIM-SM as Experimental. It was succeeded by RFC 4601 and RFC 5059, which incorporated lessons learned from early deployments and clarified protocol details. The core mechanisms—shared trees, source-specific trees, Rendezvous Points, and Join/Prune signaling—remained the foundation for the standard protocol.
sections.eli5: PIM-SM can talk to other kinds of multicast routers at network borders. This early version worked well but was refined in later RFCs.
